newsitem.title: UK: Currency board alone not panacea for Bulgaria - CSFB. [CORRECTED 10:36 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Currency board alone not panacea for Bulgaria - CSFB. [CORRECTED 10:36 GMT]

text.p: A currency board will improve confidence in the Bulgarian currency but is not sufficient to rescue the economy, CS First Boston chief East Europe economist Jonathan Hoffman said in a research note.

"It can certainly act as a catalyst for the rehabilitation of the lev, but not unless the government commits to reform in other areas - especially as regards corporate restructuring and provatisation, and the adoption of investor friendly policies - in a way that has hitherto been conspicuously absent," Hoffman said.

The International Monetary Fund has indicated that it will resume loans to Bulgaria if it adopts a currency board, a measure which ties a country's monetary base to the overall surplus or deficit of autonomous transactions on the balance of payments, hence constraining the expansion of base money.
The measure means that the central bank is not allowed to print money to finance the budget deficit and removes its independence.

"However, it does not enforce fiscal discipline in other ways - for example the government of a country with a currency board can still compel its banks to hold government paper at sub-market yields," Hoffman notes.

He said the Bulgarian people appear to welcome the currency board as a "deus ex machina" which will prevent the government from printing money, entail lending by institutions such as the IMF and enable Bulgaria to catch the leading regional economies.
To implement a currency board, Bulgaria will need external support in the region of $800 million, some of which could come from the delayed $500 million of the IMF standby.

Even with support from the IMF and others, Bulgaria already faces a tough budget with 60 percent of spending on debt servicing and a currency board will exacerbate that because the central bank will not be able to print money, Hoffman warns.

"Even with a currency board, then, it is possible that things could get worse before they get better. A 1997 crisis could trigger early elections which - on current showing - would return the (opposition) Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) to power," he said. (Corrects standing of UDF from "ruling" to "opposition")
